stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist is directed by her employer to perform an administration technique that pharmacists in the Commonwealth are generally authorised to perform. She has never been trained in that technique and has never performed it. What governs her decision?

choices.text: She may proceed, because the act sits within the recognised pharmacist scope.
She may proceed, because her employer has directed her to perform it.
She may proceed if a colleague who is trained in it observes her doing it.
She may not proceed unless the Board grants her an individual authorisation.
She may not proceed, because it is outside her own training and experience.

explanation.core_reasoning: 247 CMR 9.01(4) requires a pharmacist to practise within the scope of his or her own education, training and experience AND within the recognized pharmacist scope of practice. Both limbs must be satisfied, so an act well inside the profession's scope may still be outside the scope of a pharmacist who has never been trained in it.

choice_analysis.A: That satisfies the second limb only.
choice_analysis.B: An employer direction cannot supply training and experience.
choice_analysis.C: Observation by a colleague is not the regulatory test.
choice_analysis.D: No individual Board authorisation is contemplated; training and experience are the test.
choice_analysis.E: Correct: the individual competence limb is not met.

related_facts: The same regulation governs every act of pharmacy practice
explanation.mpje_trap: Candidates decide scope questions at the level of the profession and never descend to the individual.

reasoning_steps: Note that the regulation states two cumulative limbs
Confirm the act is within the profession's scope
Test it against this pharmacist's own training and experience
